result.summary: Neptune and Triton call back the floodwaters, and the land reappears. Deucalion and Pyrrha, the only survivors, rest on Parnassus and Deucalion laments that they alone are left of mankind.

scenes.title: The Flood Recedes
scenes.summary: Jupiter clears the clouds, Neptune lays down his trident and has Triton blow his shell to recall the waters. The seas and rivers return to their beds and the land emerges.

scenes.title: Deucalion's Lament
scenes.summary: Deucalion weeps over the empty world and tells Pyrrha they are the whole human race. He wishes he could remake the people lost.
scenes.stakes: Their survival is uncertain and they face lonely despair as the last humans.

alias_notes.explanation: A title for the sea god, who lays aside his trident.

notable_quotes.reason: Deucalion sums up humanity reduced to two survivors, 'mere samples of mankind'.

analysis.text: The passage shows divine punishment giving way to restoration, with the just pair spared and the world beginning again.
The flood story parallels Near Eastern accounts such as Gilgamesh and Noah, adapted to Greek myth with Deucalion on Parnassus.

legacy.text: Deucalion and Pyrrha became the Greek flood survivors, and Ovid's version influenced later retellings of the myth in European art and literature.

fun_facts.text: Parnassus, where the ark lands, was sacred to Apollo and the Muses and later became a symbol of poetry.

language_notes.text: Phocis, Aonia (Boeotia) and Actæa (Attica) are regions of central Greece; the flood covers the land between them.
The Corycian Nymphs were nymphs of the Corycian cave on Parnassus, sacred to local worship.
"The partner of his couch" is a periphrasis for his wife, Pyrrha.
"Azure" means sky-blue; here it describes the sea-god Triton's colouring.
"The bidden retreat" is the ordered signal to withdraw, like a military trumpet call for retreat.
Deucalion calls Pyrrha "sister" because they were cousins, both descended from the Titan Iapetus's line; hence "common origin."
His father Prometheus was said to have moulded humans from earth and clay.

context_notes.text: Parnassus is a mountain in Phocis with twin peaks, sacred to Apollo and the Muses.
Themis was a goddess of divine law and justice, here holding the oracle at Parnassus before Apollo.
Jupiter sent the flood to punish human wickedness, and spares these two for their piety.
Neptune rules the sea and carries a trident; Triton is his son and herald, who blows a conch shell.

literary_notes.text: Calling the whole land "a wide plain of sudden waters" conveys the flood's total scale, turning fertile country into sea.
The repeated "sees that but one... remains out of so many thousands" stresses how few survive and why Jupiter relents.
The shell's call is obeyed by the waters as if they were soldiers hearing a command.
The silent, empty earth and Deucalion's tearful address to Pyrrha evoke the loneliness of the last survivors.
Calling themselves "samples of mankind" shrinks humanity to a sample pair, expressing the couple's humility and loss.
